utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. There being no preliminaries, may the witness please be called in. And while the witness is coming in, we just deal with one matter. But before we do that, just to announce that the Chamber today is sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis. Due to urgent Tribunal business, Judge Orie is not able to be with us today. Okay. Now deal with this one matter that we have to deal with. On the 3rd of May, 2013, the Prosecution filed a motion seeking to amend the status of RM297 from Rule 92 bis to Rule 92 ter and the status of Witness RM324 [Realtime transcript read in error "RM3"] from Rule 92 ter to Rule 92 bis. In its motion the Prosecution submits that it has discussed the status change with the Defence and that the Defence does not object. The Defence will, the Prosecution submits, withdraw any previous objections to that admission of the Rule 92 ter statements for both witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, does this reflect accurately the position of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have a few seconds. I have to check the numbers. I don't know the names by heart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can tell us later. Thank you so much. Okay, we wait for you. Good morning, Mr. Franken.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Again, I must apologise for the fact that you walked in while we were attending to some other business which doesn't concern you. Just to remind you, Mr. Franken, that you still bound by the declaration that you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am aware of that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Franken. Mr. Stojanovic, are you ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before my colleague starts, only in transcript I don't have the other number. It just says "3."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The one is 324.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you are ready, Mr. Stojanovic. All right. Mr. Stojanovic, you were dealing with P1147 when we adjourned yesterday. Do you want it on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, I would appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May we have that on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. If you recall, yesterday we left off during the viewing of clips from the video recording of what we call the first meeting held in Fontana on the 11th of July, 1995. Since we have one more clip to see, I would kindly ask for it to be played, and after that, I have a few questions for you relating to the basic subject of our discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So can we please play a clip from P1147, starting at 59:10, an ends at 00: --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1:03:25.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "I have a question. "Yes. "What can I say to General Nicolai after we have met here tonight? "You don't have too much good of the conversation with General Nicolai. He cannot help you, either you nor the Muslim population. But if you do insist, anyway, you tell him ... UNPROFOR troops, no matter of the air strikes, no matter what, your soldiers shooting at my soldiers are not the goal of mine. Every one of you and your soldiers have only one life. And I do not believe that you would like to leave it here. That's why I ask for absolute co-operation. The goal of my action is also not the Muslim civilian population. I want to help you, even though you do not deserve it. Not as a human nor as an officer, but I will do this because of those children of UNPROFOR. Because I wouldn't like their mothers to welcome them in coffins. I also want to help that Muslim civilian population which is also not to be blamed for what happened. That's why I would like to ask you the next thing. Are you able and when would -- when would you be able to bring here representatives of civilian population? I would have an arrangement with them ... from here, you can go out, all of you, or stay, all of you, or die, all of you. And I wouldn't like you to die. If Muslim army in Srebrenica wants to talk, you may bring some of their representatives. If it's possible that that ... by your estimation that one that is the main authority there, and I know that Naser Oric is not there. At that meeting, I'm expecting we can agree that all this stops, and that problem of civilian population, Muslim army and your soldiers is resolved in a peaceful way. You have my guarantees for organising such a meeting and for the people you will bring here. Are you able to do it tonight?"

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Franken, this is, I would say, the address of General Mladic at this first meeting which summarises everything that had been discussed beforehand. My question is: Did you have an opportunity to see this video-clip or video recording of this first meeting in the past?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to this extent. I saw one clip where the toast was, but further on, it's new to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Based on what you saw yesterday and today, did you ever notice or hear that General Mladic issued any threats with regard to the shelling of the UNPROFOR compound in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I understand that this is just a part of that meeting, what is recorded. So -- Secondly, literally, I didn't hear Mladic say anything about, If you not, then we will shell, in this footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear, based on these video-clips shown to you - and I understand the restrictions that you are facing - did General Mladic, at any point, indicate to Colonel Karremans that he might target and shoot on the Muslim civilian population?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not literally, but there were some threats in this -- in this footage. I remember Mladic saying in the last footage, in the last clip, that there were three possibilities: Stay, go away, or die. He said in another clip that the POWs, if not, then would be no guests anymore. So there were some threats but not given better content.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear any threat at all aimed at the civilian population? Or maybe you did answer my question, but I didn't receive it.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did answer, because I believe in the last clip Mladic says that there are three possibilities. I repeat what I said before: One was you can stay, you can go, or you can die. And in the text before that, it's obvious that he meant with "they" or "you" the population and DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And, finally, during these video-clips did you hear from General Mladic any threats aimed at members of the Dutch battalion that were in this hotel on that particular evening and who had arrived from their observation posts?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He said somewhere in -- in -- in one of the clips before, he said that the POWs, if - and I don't exactly remember the words - but if we didn't co-operate or if we didn't stop opposing the VRS, the POWs wouldn't be treated anymore as a guest or words of that content.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the last clip, General Mladic says - and I'm going to quote him: "UNPROFOR forces, despite the air strikes by NATO, and the activities aimed at my forces by your forces, are still not the target of my activities in the military sense of the word." So if you are told something of that nature by the head of the army that you are talking to, would you take that as a clear indication that UNPROFOR forces were not the target of his operations?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite clear that he said that. That doesn't take away the fact that on your previous question if I heard any threats in -- in the -- in the speaking, in the speech of General Mladic, well, I heard threats, and whether or not the objective of his actions were the DutchBat III is, as far as I'm concerned, concerning the threats he said, he told about, is not relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that after the 11th of July, the evening of the 11th of July, there was never any shelling of the Potocari compound? After the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The fact is that what General Mladic said materialised in the way that he described on the evening of the 11th.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What -- what's your question? What? Do you want me to confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Just to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you be so kind to tell me this. But, first of all, let us look at document D280. That's your statement that we used yesterday as well, dated the 22nd July 1995, which you gave at the Pleso base. And if we can look at page 4 in the B/C/S and that would be paragraph 5, and page 6 in the English version, the penultimate paragraph. This refers to the evacuation of the population. So in the English, it's page 6, the penultimate paragraph. Thank you. And it reads, these are your words: "It was agreed with Mladic that UNPROFOR would supervise it. Our role was to provide as much presence as possible and to escort them. The men were separated from the women. The Muslims agreed to let the men be investigated for war crimes, under the supervision of the UNHCR and the Red Cross may be investigated. Note: Franken says he is in the possession of the English and Bosnian text of the agreement with Mladic. He himself acted on the basis of an oral translation by his interpreter." Let me ask you this with regard to this passage. It says that the Muslims had agreed that the men suspected of war crimes may be interrogated under the supervision of the UNHCR and the Red Cross. Can you please explain to us what was the source of this statement of yours?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first, I think UNHCR is incorrect and should have been UN. And I do not remember the source. This statement is from 1995, but I don't recollect the source. I know that -- sorry. I don't remember what the source was, but there must have been a source because I didn't think it up myself. I can't say what source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would the source not be the agreement itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could have been, Your Honour, but I don't really remember. I can't indicate a source, whether it's agreement verbal message, guide-line of Colonel Karremans or whatever. I do not really remember. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put a follow-up question. It is written here "the Muslims agreed." Who are "the Muslims"? Who are you referring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that refers to the committee - we formed representatives of the Muslims - and that's what I'm referring to with "the Muslims."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The committee is the people who participated in the Hotel Fontana meeting; is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correctly understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I might just clear one thing with you, Mr. Franken. Is this statement as it stands, "are these your words." When Mr. Stojanovic started reading he said, "these are your words." And then, of course, the second sentence says "our role was," which gives the impression that these are indeed your words. But further down in the bracket they say N. B. Franken says he is -- now the third person is no longer the third person. Are you able to tell us whether these are your words or somebody is just writing this and you are also one of those people who are being written about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it is a -- a -- how do you say that? During these interviews, et cetera, there was -- notes were made and later on those made -- those notes were more or less formed to a text. Whether these were literally my words, I don't know, but it is the contents and the intention of the words are correct. Is that an answer, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is an answer. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But I have another question exactly in relation to this. When this text was formulated, did you have the opportunity to read it later and to confirm that these words are correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is -- sorry, again this is the 1995 debriefing report. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That is what I understood from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, we didn't have the text back to verify that and to put it -- a signature under it as being the correct text. We did not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: With respect to what you said, can we please look at 1D84, page 387. That's actually two pages from the book entitled: "The Planned Chaos," authored by Ibran Mustafic. Before we look at it, let me ask you if you recall the person named Ibran Mustafic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I were to recall and remind you that that was a SDA deputy in the Assembly of BH before the war, and who was the subject of two assassination attempts in the Srebrenica enclave, does this name of Ibran Mustafic now ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And you say to remind me, but I can't be reminded because the name doesn't say me anything, doesn't ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to read this portion and then put a question to you. The English page is good. We need the last paragraph, in which he says, describing the events of Potocari which he witnessed himself because he was there: "At that time a check-point was set up on the little bridge across the Rabin creek and manned by Chetniks. Several soldiers of the Dutch battalion, Nesib Mandzic, Ibro Nuhanovic and Camil were together letting through and separating the people. I knew they had been in Bratunac attending negotiations but I could not believe my eyes that I was seeing that several Dutch soldiers were working together with the Chetniks on separating people, including Nesib, Ibro and Camil." Mr. Franken, these three names are the negotiators who attended the meeting in the Fontana hotel on the morning of the 12th of July. One of them is a signatory of the statement dated the 17th of July, 1995, that you had an opportunity to see. Did you have any information that could serve as a basis for the statement that you made, to the effect that the Muslims had agreed that the men suspected of war crimes may be interrogated under the supervision of the UNHCR and the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the information I had about that was the debriefing of one of the meetings where it was discussed and obviously General Mladic told the DutchBat and the committee that he wanted to interrogate the -- the able men. The event described in this paragraph of that book you shown me, a simple comment: No way. There's no way that Dutch soldiers were actually separating men and women together with the VRS. That happened always when we left the secure area we had outside our compound, by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any information to the effect that these three negotiators were, in fact, at the check-point, in order to identify individuals who were supposed to be separated and checked whether they had participated in some crime or not, as it is stated in this book?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Again, this may have more fairly been a matter put to the individuals that are being asked about here. Now earlier when my colleague was asking about DutchBat, that is a witness perhaps -- that is a matter perhaps appropriate for this witness. But if this -- these -- the current issue, if that has not been put before, I'm not sure how much more light this witness can shed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my question was straightforward: Does Mr. Franken have such information about the role that these three persons had in the activities to do with the identification of the people who were being separated. Nothing more, nothing less. So does he or doesn't he have the information?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The observation is overruled. [Microphone not activated] you may put the question again, Mr. Stojanovic, for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Franken, I will reiterate my question. Did you have any information, as it is quoted in this book, to the effect that these three negotiators at any point in time took part in identifying and recognising, identifying men and their separation at the check-point?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have information that they took part, but I think I know what event is wrongly described in this book. And to take you back, when I decided to make the list of men within our security, we tried to register the men outside the compound as well, so not on our base. Then those three people went out to start registering the men. They were seen and probably identified by the VRS, and there was a row, et cetera. The effect was that the lady completely had a nervous breakdown and had to be taken as a patient into the hospital. And I think that's the only event wrongly described in this book that those three were together out. Because after that, they didn't have the guts to get out of the gate anymore so we could not register the men in the outside -- outside the compound. I think he describes that event but gives the wrong explanation for the people being there. Is that an answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, is it correct that there were men, both in Potocari and at the compound, who refused to be registered for some reason?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recollect well, within the compound, there were 60 or 70 men who didn't want to be registered. I don't have numbers of men who didn't want to be registered outside the compound because the effort or the attempt to register them failed, as I described to you shortly before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How did you interpret their refusal to be registered and be, as you said, given a name, an identity?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. I took it for granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And we can agree that this activity and this idea of yours, in fact, was not well received by the refugee -- refugees, the men, who were in Potocari outside the compound.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I do not know, because in the -- the beginning of the attempt to register them and to tell them what we wanted with it, there was that incident with the VRS with the result for the lady, as described, and the fact that the two men didn't have the guts anymore to go outside the gate. So I don't know how many outside the compound would have refused to be registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But, in the end, there was never a list compiled of men who were outside of the compound; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you tell the Trial Chamber, please, when the separation of the men from the women started? Could you give us the hour and the date, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seeing the fact that the evacuation started on the 12th at about half past 12.00, 1230, 1300. Didn't happen on the first convoy; the end of the second. So it would have been the -- the organised start of it would have been around, let's say, 1400 hours. But that's an estimation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So, on the 12th of July, around 1400 hours, as far as you can assess?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please pull up in e-court a document that we used yesterday. Unfortunately, Your Honours, I think I failed to note down the D number, but the 65 ter number -- it's actually a transcript dated 11th November 2002, a parliamentary commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The minutes of the parliamentary commission. The 65 ter number is 19420.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Simply for some reason, I failed to note it down yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The correct 65 ter number is 19425.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to refer you to page 505 in the English. That's page 505 in English. And, in B/C/S, that's page 60. 6-0.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is only three-page document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I requested the transcript of 11th November 2002, and my apologies, but that was 1D937. 937. My apologies. 1D937. That's a document that we used yesterday in hard copy. It's -- the original is in English, and Your Honours, I believe you have it before you. My apologies. I would need page 60 in the B/C/S version, and in the English version, the last three digits are 505. Thank you. This is the document before us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you proceed, Mr. Shin, you were on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. It was merely to assist my colleague in identifying the correct document that he had wanted. But while I'm on my feet I would just note that I believe my colleague may have referred to the original being in English, but I believe the original may have been in Dutch. The English is a translation as well, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And at the moment, we don't have this on the screen. There's a different document. On the screen, I see an interview with the witness dated 31st of March, 1999. But you are referring to a hearing of 11th of November, 2002. Did you manage to upload it in the meantime? We discussed the process of uploading. Oh, now I -- it seems to be on the screen. But you need another page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you indicate the page you need again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's page 47 in the English, in e-court. Page 47, the middle of the page. And the B/C/S page that we have before us is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't have English in e-court. It's only Dutch and B/C/S uploaded in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that sense, Your Honour, I suggest that perhaps we could provide the witness the hard copy. And perhaps the Trial Chamber can use the hard copy because we have not been able to upload it into e-court and that's on page 505 in the hard copy version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you provide the witness with a hard copy, Mr. Stojanovic, if you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that we did give it to the witness yesterday, but I do have another copy here. And I would appreciate the assistance of the Court Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In this document, in this interview before parliamentary committee, you say the following: "Could you tell us why you did not -- why you refused to help with the evacuation?" And you answer as follows: "I've already described the situation the people found themselves in. These were not rested and we well-fed citizens, resting before being deported. When they arrived with us they were in poor condition already. I could not have foreseen this. This has to do with what I had said about medical assistance, sanitary conditions and similar. Mladic offered the UN to carry this out themselves, but the UN said that they weren't able to do that and they then gave the go-ahead to Mladic to do it, and that's how it transpired. Of course, had we been able to consider some other manner to ensure that these people arrived safely and soundly to a safe location as soon as possible and as comfortably as possible with the best possible escort, that is my answer to your question." Mr. Franken, do you stand by what you said then in response to the question put by Mrs. De Vries?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's note: We do not have the English version before us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, the interpreters note that they don't have a copy before them. I think it would be helpful if you gave them a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. But do I have to do it right away?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know whether you're going to read from this document. If you are, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, there's nothing more that I will read. It was just this excerpt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague just informed me that we have actually uploaded this into e-court, the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's 65 ter 19425. And there is an English version --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you called 19425 a few minutes ago, which we told you was D278. You discovered that was the wrong document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should put your question to the witness and deal with another document after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Franken, my question was: Do you stand by the answer that you provided to the parliamentary committee on the 11th of November, 2002?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But just one remark, your question originally was: Why did you refuse to co-operate or to assist the evacuation. That is incorrect. We did not refuse. Simply we were soldiers and we got the order to assist in the evacuation by the UN, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just to clarify this matter, the question of Ms. De Vries from this parliamentary committee was, and I quote: "Can you indicate why you did not refuse to help carry out the evacuation?" That was the question I think Mr. Stojanovic was referring to, that question of this member of the parliament.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will conclude with a question, and I'm referring to this excerpt.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You said here that the UN said that they were unable to carry out this evacuation so they gave the go-ahead to Mladic. When you say the UN, whom do you actually refer to? Who was it who approved the aforementioned evacuation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This information I -- came to me through Colonel Karremans who had the contacts in that time to BH Command in Sarajevo. He told me that he said -- he asked the UN or BH Command to arrange that. They gave the answer that they were not able to do so. On that occasion, they all -- they also said the battalion should do it himself. Probably not either -- just forgetting that we didn't have any fuel to drive any car. Then, in the end, it was, Okay, let the VRS do it with their means. But that's information that came to me through Colonel Karremans.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that at one point in time you were asked whether you could organise the evacuation with the resources that you had and that it was your assessment in view of the number of vehicles that you had and the number of refugees, and the very difficult humanitarian situation and the difficulty of feeding all these people, the Dutch battalion was, objectively speaking, unable to carry out this evacuation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, we've just asked this question to the witness a few minutes ago. He has answered it. You're asking it a second time, in different words. Can you please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Could we now take a look, document 65 ter 19420, and I believe this is a document I mentioned earlier. That's 65 ter 19420. And if we could have the B/C/S version --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Franken, this is your statement on the 13th of September, 1995; statement you provided -- gave to the Dutch army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we have page 4 in B/C/S, please, and page 4 in English, the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is no B/C/s version of this document in e-court, if it's 19420.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Madam Registrar, we couldn't hear you. Could you repeat what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 19420 does not have a B/C/S version. It's only Dutch and English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will only ask you this, because you have both the Dutch and the English version before you, so I'll just ask you this, Mr. Franken: In this statement you say that according to the agreement on the evacuation of refugees, UNPROFOR was supposed to supply the fuel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where are you reading, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 4, the last paragraph in English, Your Honour. The one that we have before us. And it will go over to page 5, the last two lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So what you said in this interview was this: "The agreement on the evacuation of refugees stated that UNPROFOR would supply the fuel. Whether Smith or Karremans had made this arrangement, he did not know. Because there was a fuel shortage in the battalion, Mladic supplied it himself initially, and there was talk on an arrangement (in exchange for its use) later on. It was striking that the Serbs, when the 30.000 litres were delivered in Bratunac, only took what they had agreed upon and to everyone's surprise left the rest behind in the fuel truck." The first thing I want to ask you is this: Can you recall the date when these 30.000 litres of fuel were delivered to Bratunac? What day was it, and when did the VRS take over the fuel?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just thinking the date for -- as far as your second question is, the -- the fuel truck was stopped at OP-Papa and I was informed he was there. And the VRS said, Okay, we are entitled to a part of that and I agreed to that, sent an officer along, and they exactly took out what was agreed upon, what I believe is 27.000 litres. The date will have been, if I recollect well, 16th of July, but that is without guarantee. As far as I recollect, this was the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now this fact that the fuel that was supplied for the vehicles for the evacuation was supposed to be supplied through UNPROFOR, that was the result of agreement between General Mladic and General Smith; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I stated before, I don't know between which persons that agreement was. The only thing I know that I -- through Colonel Karremans, I got the order to supply the -- a -- applicable amount of diesel to the VRS concerning the diesel consumption during the evacuation performed by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that the decision on the evacuation was taken at UNPROFOR level and that the implementation of the decision was by the VRS because the Dutch battalion did not have the resources to carry it out?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether that decision was a decision of -- thought of by UNPROFOR itself or being the only possible decision seeing the situation and the fact that the implementation, the actual transport of the refugee -- sorry, of the population to the Kladanj area is correct. That -- that was with the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I would like us to take a look together at P1166. That is the agreement between General Smith and General Mladic that you've already testified about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I just need your instruction, Your Honour, whether I should go on with this after the break or can I go on before the break with the questions that relate to this document. And I believe after the break I will need about 15 minutes to wrap up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, didn't you indicate that you need only an hour today?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. But I believe I will need an additional 15 minutes or so. And that is still within the three hours that I originally requested. I was mistaken yesterday when I thought that I would finish in an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much. Then we will take a break and maybe you must continue after the break. May the witness please be escorted out. We'll come back in 20 minutes' time, Mr. Franken.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break at come back at ten to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Sorry. May the witness please be escorted into the courtroom, I said. And while we're waiting for the witness, Mr. Lukic, are you able to answer that question that we asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think my learned friend Mr. McCloskey is with us to clarify the thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, but the Chamber needs your response.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Unless Mr. McCloskey has got your brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My response is that there is some, I think, misunderstanding whether it is 92 bis or 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You talk with Mr. McCloskey and come back to us later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we did have a chance to talk about it and cleared up the issue, and I can either do that now or after the witness is done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I suggest you do that after the witness is done. Thank you so much, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Stojanovic, the witness is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Franken, I believe that we have General Smith and General Mladic's agreement before us. And I would like to ask you if you had an opportunity to see this agreement before?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is that the document that you made reference to in your statement as serving as the basis for your activities in those days in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not as the basis, because my -- our role concerning the evacuation was before, but afterwards it was a -- yeah, what you say, a consent in our acting. Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In view of your answers that I saw in the draft transcript on the page 22 and the last four lines on 21, let me ask you once again: After having seen this agreement, to the best of your recollection, at what level, or, rather, where exactly the decision was made to proceed with the evacuation of the civilian population from Potocari?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it -- it looks logical that it was done between BH Command and General Mladic, that the decision was made there, as I stated more or less before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And, according to the statement quoted that you stand by in its entirety, you said that it was offered to Mladic to do it themselves because the UN said that they didn't have the capacity and then gave consent for Mladic to undertake that, were you referring to General Smith specifically, or were you referring to any other UN institution instead?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I stated that before. This information I got through Colonel Karremans, and what his source was exactly, I do not know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Can we please just take a look and comment one portion of your statement of 31st of March, 1999. That's D278. Paragraph 30 in both the B/C/S and English versions. And while we are waiting for it to be uploaded --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, there's only Dutch and English versions of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct. Thank you. I would appreciate if we can have both versions for the benefit of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My question is: Mr. Franken, would it be consistent with the rules that in case of POWs, during war time, as the case was in Srebrenica, indeed, would it be necessary and possible to carry out the procedure of screening in order to detect whether amongst them were the people suspected of war crimes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the normal procedure is when you have, as I stated before, if you have a big group of potential prisoners or people in war time, you start dividing them in civilians and military, and you separate them. The aspect of war crimes is in that procedure not mentioned, so that is not completely correct. The -- dividing the group into men and women and children and elderly men, et cetera, is normal, it's normal procedure. That's what we learned our soldiers as well. But the aspect of war crimes doesn't have a role in that procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 30 that you can see before you, it is said: "When the men and women were separated, Franken challenged the commander in question ... but he invoked the Geneva Conventions with regard to treatment of prisoner of war. Franken asked us, 'What was I supposed to do?' The Serb promised to treat the ABiH soldiers in accordance with the Geneva Conventions, and thereby, in fact, complying with normal obligations." Your previous answer, does it correspond to what you said in paragraph 30?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is consistent with each other. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So the initial step in separating the able-bodied men from the whole crowd of population would not basically constitute anything disputable, from the point of view of the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. It is a variation on the theme because normally you separated the uniformed, the combatants, recognisable combatants from the group. In this case, it is a variation because all able-bodied men could have been combatant. So it is not -- there's nothing wrong with that procedure in itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I will finish with one question. Yesterday, you will remember being shown a photograph that confirmed your recollection that the personal belongings that had been left in front of the white house were set on fire. Now I'm asking you: Do you remember that among these personal belongings, weapons, ammunitions were found and that there were detonations during the process of setting them on fire?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether anything was found between those belongings, I do not know of. I know that there were some -- some bangs when they were set on fire, some explosions as you say it. But it doesn't mean that it was ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to decide what caused the explosions when these things were set on fire?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And I will finish with the document that you talked about during examination-in-chief, specifically the list of men who were in the -- the UNPROFOR base. Can you tell the Trial Chamber to whom was this list forwarded and has it ever arrived to the recipient that you intended to send it to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The list was forwarded to HQ sector north-east Tuzla BH Command, Sarajevo, the Dutch Crisis Staff that was an element of the Dutch commanding -- General Staff here in Holland. And, no, that was it, those three addressees. I know that, in fact, it was received here in Holland because when I was back in Holland quite some time, it was reproduced from some bureau here in the General Staff office. Whether it really came to Tuzla or BH Command, I do not know of. I did not get a -- from any officer, or what, a receipt or confirmation of the receipt of that passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to your estimate, how many able-bodied men in the course of these two days were separated from this crowd of refugees?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you know, we made an estimate -- we knew pretty good how many men there were within the compound. There was an estimation of the men outside the compound, and that total is, if I recollect well, an amount of about 1.000 able-bodied men, and they were separated, with one exception: First convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I've been asked to put just one more question to you, Mr. Franken. Do you know that in the area where the crash of the helicopter took place, which is the general area of Zlovrh and Brloske mountains, do you know if two bodies were buried there which remained on the location after your departure? Do you have any information about that and who these individuals were, these two bodies?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On both questions, no. I did not have the information so I didn't know or had any information about the identity of the -- of the victims, of the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Franken, thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, before you sit down, Exhibit D278 has only the Dutch -- Dutch original and English translation. There's no B/C/S translation. Are we likely to get that? I see Mr. Shin is standing up. Yes, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. If we could assist, there does exist a B/C/S translation. We have already undertaken steps under the guidance of Ms. Stewart to get that uploaded, and we will be able to inform you as soon as that has been done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please do so. Thank you very much, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you and thanks to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any re-examination, Mr. Shin?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, just brief. I will be less than ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you start, I would like to put two follow-up questions to the last topics, one of the last topics mentioned by Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Franken, you gave us an indication about 1.000 able bodied men separated from the other population. These 1.000 were they inside of the compound or outside? Or both together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is together, Your Honour. There were about 300 within the compound. We knew that of -- trying to compose that list you know about, and the number on the outside was estimated in the crowd. Just an estimation, so many men, approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Approximately 700 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. 6- to 700 was the estimation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: My last question relates again to the pile of bags and other belongings set on fire. Did anybody tell you why these things were set on fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. I remember that one of my officers asked a Serb officer and didn't get an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would just begin with an update on my last remarks on D278. The B/C/S translation is now uploaded, so that is available in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, will you please attach that translation, the B/C/S translation, to the exhibit. Yes, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And just one -- I would just point Your Honours to paragraph 112 of the statement of this witness where he addresses -- I'm sorry, 113 where he addresses the breakdown of men inside the compound and outside. I'm sorry, the statement does have a P number now as I'm correctly reminded. It's P1417. It is the amalgamated statement and just to assist Your Honours with that last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If I may proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Colonel Franken, if I could begin first with the document we just had on the screen a minute ago; this is D278. My -- my colleague, Mr. Stojanovic had asked you -- had read out to you paragraph 30 regarding the separation of men and women. We also see there a specific list says: "Franken challenged the commander in question." Just so that the picture is clear for this Trial Chamber, can you recall who this commander in question was and you may wish to refer to paragraphs -- the two paragraphs above that, 28 and 29. You may want to read that to refresh your recollection, if necessary. If I could please have the page 3 -- I'm sorry, page 2 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please let me read it first. Yes. The person is indeed Colonel Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And Colonel Jankovic in paragraph 28 -- I'm sorry, paragraph 28 here, you refer to him as "assistant of Mladic." To the best of your knowledge what was his -- his position?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: His position within the organisation of the VRS I do not know of. He indicated that he was General Staff officer from -- as I recollect, he used the word Supreme Command. And he is -- his job was to prepare and to co-ordinate the withdrawal of DutchBat itself and he was not involved in the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And just so we're clear, when you explain just now what his job was, was that something he told you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what he indicated himself, what he told me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to turn now to 65 ter 19420. Sir, you'll recognise this document because you've just been asked questions about it by my colleague Mr. Stojanovic. And I'd just like to clarify one point in the paragraph read about the fuel; this is page 4 on the English. And perhaps we'll take a moment to wait for it to come up on the screen. And you'll see in the lower half of that English page the area where you've been asked questions. Now, just before the quote, let me ask this: I just wanted to clarify the -- the fuel in question here this is fuel that UNPROFOR is providing to the Serbs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, originally that amount of fuel, as far as I know, came for DutchBat. It was stopped by the Serbs in the direct vicinity of OP-Papa yellow bridge, then I was informed that the fuel was there and they wanted their share of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. So if we look at just the provision at the first line of the last paragraph which is the line just preceding what Mr. Stojanovic had read, it states here: "Franken stated the following with regard to the diesel provided to the Serbs ..." So given -- with the background that you've just provided at this particular instance, this is regarding diesel that is being delivered in Bratunac to the Serbs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, from Papa the -- I ordered an officer to go with that truck and they were brought to Bratunac where it was pumped into tanks of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And one additional question here. You state that "to everyone's surprise" the rest of the fuel had been left. Why was it to everyone's surprise?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, well, that -- that is not on facts but a question of feeling. We thought really because there has been experience with the -- denying fuel, et cetera, et cetera, now there came fuel. They said we want our part and I was indeed surprised. It is a feeling that there came back about 3.000 litres being exactly the difference between the amounts they could demand, being 27.000 litres, and what was in the truck. And I was surprised, just a feeling, not on facts or not seeing the history of -- of -- of -- of denying diesel and things vanishing from convoys coming in, et cetera, we were surprised that the 3.000 litres were actually left and came to DutchBat --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution would tender 65 ter 19420 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How many pages is that, Mr. Shin?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I believe that it is -- in the English, anyway, it's a total of 23 pages, although several of the pages at the end are attachments. So we could -- we could tender pages 1 through 14 in the English which are the statement itself. The rest are attachments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Shin, only one page has been referred to in this statement and that page -- whatever came from that page has been read into the record. Do we really have to admit 14 pages that have never been talked about at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if -- this is the only document used by the Defence with this witness to challenge him that has not been tendered by the Defence. So we would take the position that it would be fair given some issues of memory recollection that a statement from the 13th of September, 1995, may assist the Trial Chamber in assessing the credibility of the witness, not necessarily those other pages for the substance contained therein but to assess the credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Read 13 pages to assess the credibility of the witness on one page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: It does cover other aspects of the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think the Chamber will order that only this page be admitted, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I ask a couple of more questions about this document to the witness in case -- to establish a foundation should the Prosecution seek to tender this document at a later point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] you may proceed, Mr. Shin. Sorry, apparently my microphone was not activated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Colonel Franken, you will recall that this document as has been earlier discussed was from the 13th of September, 1995. Would your memory of some of the events talked -- discussed therein have been more clear at that point than it is now?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, well, that's almost human. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And have you had a chance to review the materials -- I'm sorry, this document itself after it was prepared?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the debriefing in September 1995. No, we were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If I could perhaps refresh your mind as to one thing, if I could turn to page 13 of the English, at the bottom. And -- yes. At the very bottom we see there that -- well, I won't read the whole thing, but it states that you signed it as correct. Is that correct that -- would that be right that you signed this?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my recollection I did not. But it says here I did. Well, we had that many debriefings, reviews and things that obviously I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And just --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it. I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes. Just to be clear, on the left we do see the original. That is your signature; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: The witness is a Bosnian Muslim who was in Srebrenica in July 1995. As Bosnian Serb forces began entering Srebrenica on 11 July 1995, the witness joined the column of Muslim men fleeing the Srebrenica enclave and heading towards Muslim-held territory. On 13 July 1995, in the early morning hours, the witness was captured by Bosnian Serb police and transferred to the custody of officers at the MUP check-point in Konjevic Polje. He was beaten and mistreated together with other Muslim prisoners. Later that morning, the witness and other Muslim prisoners were ordered to board a bus and were taken a few kilometres up the road towards Zvornik. The prisoners were then ordered off the bus marched down an embankment, forced to line up on the banks of the Jadar river and shot by Bosnian Serb soldiers. The entire group of prisoners was executed. This witness was shot, fell into the river, was taken down by the stream and managed to survive. He eventually joined another group of fleeing Muslims and reached Muslim-held territory. That concludes the summary of the witness's evidence, Your Honours.
